Lech Lecha.title: Abraham Was a Soul Winner

blocks.t: “So Abram went, as the LORD had told him, and Lot went with him. Abram was seventy-five years old when he departed from Haran. And Abram took Sarai his wife, and Lot his brother’s son, and all their possessions that they had gathered, and the people that they had acquired in Haran, and they set out to go to the land of Canaan.” (Gen 12:4–5)

It literally says in the Hebrew text that Abraham and Sarah took “the souls that they had won in Haran, and they set out to go to the land of Canaan.” Abraham was a soul winner. It is written, “The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life, and he who wins souls is wise.” (Pr 11:30 NKJV)

Later on, when Abraham went to war against the kings who had taken Lot captive, it says, “he led forth his trained men, born in his house, 318 of them, and went in pursuit as far as Dan.” (Ge 14:14) In the traditional, English Jewish Chumash translation it says, “he armed his disciples who had been born in his house—three hundred and eighteen of them—and he pursued them as far as Dan.”

The calling to be a father and mother is not limited to having your own children. It also includes becoming parents to spiritual children by making disciples. That is what Abraham and Sarah did. God needs many such “fathers and mothers in Israel” in our time. Abraham and Sarah did not have many children of their own, but they had many disciples. They were known for their hospitality, which is described later on, in chapter 18. They invited guests and strangers into their tents, gave them delicious food and taught them about the only true God. This was how they “won souls.”

It is written, “Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers, for thereby some have entertained angels unawares.” (Heb 13:2) We know that this happened to Abraham and Sarah. (See Genesis 18.) Our homes are so important. The first believers all met in homes. They are to be houses of worship, the best environment for making disciples, training them to obey God’s commandments and walk in God’s ways. It says of Abraham, “Abraham obeyed my voice and kept my charge, my commandments, my statutes, and my laws.” (Ge 26:5) He taught his disciples to also follow these commandments.

One Jewish tradition, which should be taken with a grain of salt, says that Abraham gave all of his guests the very best food possible. While they ate together, he taught them about the only true God. If they refused to join him in giving thanks to God after they had eaten, he forced them to pay for their food.

The expressions “sons” and “disciples” are used synonymously in the Scriptures, and also in Jewish tradition. Disciples are called “sons” or “children.” This is probably how the text in Acts should be understood when it says, “Seven sons of a Jewish high priest named Sceva were doing this.” (Ac 19:14) Most likely, it is referring to seven disciples of this Jewish priest, who went around trying to cast out demons. Yeshua said to his disciples, “Little children, yet a little while I am with you.” (Jn 13:33) Both Paul and John used the same expression for their disciples. (See 1 Co 4:14, Gal 4:19, 1 Jn 2:1, and 3 Jn v.4.)

A Master and his disciples make up a “family,” or as it is also expressed, “a house.” The disciples of the most famous rabbis in the second Temple period, Hillel and Shammai, were called “the house of Hillel” and “the house of Shammai.” It says in Hebrews, “Messiah is faithful over God’s house as a son. And we are his house if indeed we hold fast our confidence and our boasting in our hope.” (Heb 3:6) We are disciples who belong to “the house of Messiah.” He is our Master.

The Great Commission involves much more than getting people to pray a prayer of salvation. It is all about making disciples, who learn to keep God’s commandments. “And Yeshua came and said to them, ‘All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you. And behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age.’” (Mt 28:18–20)

Making disciples is a time consuming enterprise that requires a lot of hard work. It is just like raising children. It takes time, much effort and much prayer. But this is what we have been commanded to do. We should get as many children of our own as possible, but we should also make many disciples. Our own children are our primary and most important disciples. It must begin with them, as it is written, “All your children shall be taught by the LORD, and great shall be the peace of your children.” (Isa 54:13)

It is never too late to begin making disciples. On the contrary, the older we get the more wisdom we have to give others. One of the rabbis in the time of Yeshua said, “Be scrupulous in your tithing and make many disciples!” These are good rules to follow. Abraham and Sara did both. They tithed (Gen 14:20), and they had many disciples (Gen 14:14).

Vayera.title: The Binding of Isaac

blocks.t: “After these things God tested Abraham and said to him, ‘Abraham!’ And he said, ‘Here am I.’ He said, ‘Take your son, your only son Isaac, whom you love, and go to the land of Moriah, and offer him there as a burnt offering on one of the mountains of which I shall tell you.’” (Gen 22:1–2)

This was the tenth and final test that Abraham, the father of all who believe, had to go through—and it was the most difficult of them all. It was the very climax in his walk of faith. God’s command seemed to be beyond all reason. Finally, the promised son had been born. Should Abraham now sacrifice his beloved son, whom he loved so much? Isaac meant everything to Abraham.

We can compare this test with Yeshua’s words to his disciples, after they had recognized him to be the long awaited the Messiah. He then told them that he must be killed and on the third day be raised again. What was Peter’s response? “Far be it from you, Lord! This shall never happen to you.” (Mt 16:22)

It is not difficult to see a parallel between the text in verse 2, ‘Take your son, your only son Isaac, whom you love,…and offer him” and John 3:16. Many Jews read Genesis 22 every time before they pray their morning prayers. It is one of the most frequently read chapter in the entire Bible among the Jewish people, the very foundation of Israel’s relationship with God.

Abraham did not hesitate. He knew that it was God who had spoken to him and he had learnt to trust Him, so he obeyed since he had a covenant with God. The next verse says, “So Abraham rose early in the morning, saddled his donkey, and took two of his young men with him, and his son Isaac. And he cut the wood for the burnt offering and arose and went to the place of which God had told him.” (v. 3)

Notice that God had told him about a special place. The following verse gives us another insight into why Abraham obeyed. It reads, “On the third day Abraham lifted up his eyes and saw the place from afar.” (v. 4) What did Abraham see when he lifted up his eyes? It says that he saw “the place”. “The place” is in Hebrew ha-makom (הַמָּקוֹם). It is mentioned three times in this chapter, in verses 3, 4 and 9. Ha-makom is an important word in the Scriptures, used about the place where God dwells and reveals Himself.

Abraham saw “the place” from afar on the third day. “The third day” in the Scriptures always refers to the resurrection. Yeshua explained this to his disciples after his resurrection. “Then he opened their minds to understand the Scriptures, and said to them, ‘Thus it is written, that the Messiah should suffer and on the third day rise from the dead.” (Lk 24:45–46) According to Yeshua, this is the summary of all the Scriptures.
The Book of Hebrews confirms to us what Abraham saw,

“By faith Abraham, when he was tested, offered up Isaac, and he who had received the promises was in the act of offering up his only son, of whom it was said, ‘Through Isaac shall your offspring be named.’ He considered that God was able even to raise him from the dead, from which, figuratively speaking, he did receive him back.” (Heb 11:17–19)

When Abraham lifted his eyes on the third day, he saw in the distance Golgotha and the resurrection of the Messiah two thousand years in advance! Further on in the story, Abraham told Isaac, “God will provide for himself the lamb for a burnt offering, my son.” (v. 8)
“And Abraham took the wood of the burnt offering and laid it on Isaac his son. And he took in his hand the fire and the knife. So they went both of them together.” (v. 6)

It is important to note in the text, not only Abraham’s obedience, but also Isaac’s complete obedience and surrender to his father. This is repeated again in verse 8, “So they went both of them together.” Isaac was at this time at least 30 years old. He was probably just as old as the Messiah was when he prayed in the garden, “My Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will.” (Mt 26:39)

The Hebrew root word for “the wood” that Abraham placed on Isaac is the same as the one used about the cross that Yeshua carried on his back. “…and he went out, bearing his own cross, to the place called the place of a skull, which in Aramaic is called Golgotha.” (Jn 19:17)
“When they came to the place of which God had told him, Abraham built the altar there and laid the wood in order and bound Isaac his son and laid him on the altar, on top of the wood.” (v. 9)

Among the Jewish people, this whole passage is called “the binding of Isaac” or just “the binding.” The Hebrew word that is used is akedah (עֲקֵדָה). This is the only time that this form of the word occurs in the Scriptures. According to Rashi, the word means that the hands and feet of Isaac were tied behind his back and they were tied so hard that it left marks on Isaac’s hands and feet. It is obvious that the old man Abraham could not have done this to Isaac without his consent. He submitted to his father all the way unto death. The binding of Isaac was a unique event pointing forward to the most unique event in human history: the sacrifice of Messiah at Golgotha!

Chayei Sarah.title: Sarah’s Death

blocks.t: “Sarah lived 127 years; these were the years of the life of Sarah. And Sarah died at Kiriath-arba (that is, Hebron) in the land of Canaan, and Abraham went in to mourn for Sarah and to weep for her.” (Gen 23:1-2)

Yeshua said, “For all the Prophets and the Law prophesied until John.” (Matt 11:13) This does not mean that everything in the Torah was fulfilled by the time John came, but it means that the Torah and the prophets began to be fulfilled at that time. The Torah still prophesies. It will do so as long as heaven and earth exist (Mt 5:17-18 and Lk 16:16-17). It is written in the book of Hebrews “…the law has a shadow of the good things to come.” (Heb 10:1, revised translation). Everything in the Torah has not been fulfilled yet.
This week’s Torah portion is about two women—Sarah and Rebekah. We are going to take a look at the prophetic spiritual truths revealed in lives of these two women.

The previous chapter ended with the account of the binding of Isaac, and this portion begins by speaking about Sarah’s death. Jewish tradition holds that Sarah died from the shock of hearing that Abraham had gone to sacrifice Isaac. In any case, Abraham was not there when she died, for it says that he came to mourn for her.

There is a deeper prophetic meaning behind this connection between Sarah’s death and the binding of Isaac. As we have mentioned before, Sarah is a prophetic type of God’s heavenly design for Jerusalem. Paul wrote,

“Abraham had two sons, one by a slave woman and one by a free woman. But the son of the slave was born according to the flesh, while the son of the free woman was born through promise. Now this may be interpreted allegorically: these women are two covenants. One is from Mount Sinai, bearing children for slavery; she is Hagar. Now Hagar is Mount Sinai in Arabia; she corresponds to the present Jerusalem, for she is in slavery with her children. But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother. For it is written, ‘Rejoice, O barren one who does not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who are not in labor! For the children of the desolate one will be more than those of the one who has a husband.’ Now you, brothers, like Isaac, are children of promise.” (Gal 4:22–28)

Just as Isaac was the son of Sarah, so all those who belong to Messiah are figuratively the sons of Sarah, according to Paul. It is written about Jerusalem in Psalm 87:5–7, “And of Zion it shall be said, ‘This one and that one were born in her; for the Most High himself will establish her. The Lord records as he registers the peoples; This one was born there.’ Selah. Singers and dancers alike say, ‘All my springs are in you.’”

Galatians 4:27 quotes from Isaiah 54:1. That entire chapter is speaking of the future restoration of Jerusalem. It says in verses 11–12, “O afflicted one, storm-tossed and not comforted, behold, I will set your stones in antimony, and lay your foundations with sapphires. I will make your pinnacles of agate, your gates of carbuncles, and all your wall of precious stones.” God will one day transform the present earthly Jerusalem. We can compare what is written in Isaiah 54 with the heavenly Jerusalem that John describes in the book of Revelation.

“…its radiance like a most rare jewel, like a jasper, clear as crystal. It had a great, high wall, with twelve gates, and at the gates twelve angels, and on the gates the names of the twelve tribes of the sons of Israel were inscribed…The wall was built of jasper, while the city was pure gold, like clear glass. The foundations of the wall of the city were adorned with every kind of jewel.” (Rev 21:11–12, 18–19)

It is important to understand that the heavenly Jerusalem, described in the Book of Revelation, is talking about a restored Jerusalem here on the earth. The first followers of the Messiah, Jews and Gentiles alike, all had this understanding. Their hope for the future was connected to the restoration of Jerusalem. The early church father, Justin Martyr, wrote about this in his book Dialogue with Trypho the Jew in the middle of the second century. In the book, the Rabbi Trypho at one point asks Justin,

“Do you admit as the truth, that this place Jerusalem will be rebuilt, and do you expect that your people will be regathered and rejoice with Christ, together with the patriarchs and the prophets and the saints among our people, and even those who have become proselytes before Christ came…?”

[Justin’s answer:] “I have confirmed to you before, that I and many others really hold this to be true, just as you yourself well know this …I and all other completely orthodox Christians, know that there will be a resurrection in the flesh and also a thousand years in Jerusalem, rebuilt, adorned and enlarged, as the prophets Ezekiel and Isaiah, and all of the other prophets say. And furthermore, a man among us called John, one of the apostles of Christ, prophesied in a Revelation given to him that those who had believed in our Christ, will be allowed to live in Jerusalem for a thousand years and after that the universal, that is the eternal resurrection for all will happen and also the judgment.”

According to Justin Martyr, the heavenly Jerusalem of the Book of Revelation, is the same city that Ezekiel, Isaiah and others described as a restored, earthly Jerusalem. All “orthodox Christians” during the second century had the exact same hope for the future as all Jews have had throughout history. It took at least three centuries for this biblical hope to disappear. Sarah is a picture of the restored, heavenly Jerusalem described by the prophets Ezekiel and Isaiah, and even John in the book of Revelation.

The binding of Isaac is a picture of the death and resurrection of Messiah. Just as the death of Sarah is mentioned in connection with the binding of Isaac, so Jerusalem was destroyed shortly after the death and resurrection of Yeshua. The glory vanished. Jerusalem was trampled underfoot by Gentiles and the long exile began. However, before the mention of Sarah’s death, the Torah tells of one important detail: the birth of Rebekah!

“Now after these things it was told to Abraham, ‘Behold, Milcah also has borne children to your brother Nahor: his firstborn, Buz his brother, Kemuel the father of Aram, Chesed, Hazo, Pildash, Jidlaph, and Bethuel. Bethuel fathered Rebekah.’” (Gen 22:20-23)
We will look closer at this prophetic picture later.

Toldot.title: The Birth Right

blocks.t: “Once when Jacob was cooking stew, Esau came in from the field, and he was exhausted. And Esau said to Jacob, ‘Let me eat some of that red stew, for I am exhausted!’ (Therefore his name was called Edom.) Jacob said, ‘Sell me your birthright now.’ Esau said, ‘I am about to die; of what use is a birthright to me?’ Jacob said, ‘Swear to me now.’ So he swore to him and sold his birthright to Jacob. Then Jacob gave Esau bread and lentil stew, and he ate and drank and rose and went his way. Thus Esau despised his birthright.” (Gen 25:29-34)

Why did Jacob buy the birthright from Esau? The view most people have is that Jacob was selfish and deceitful. There is, however, another, more Scriptural side to this. Remember that Jacob had been listening to the teaching and wisdom of Abraham and had heard about the promises and the calling that God had given to his descendants. Esau, on the other hand, showed no interest in this tremendous spiritual inheritance. It was the calling and the promises given to Abraham that mattered most to Jacob.

Would the right of the firstborn, to this enormous spiritual calling to be the heir of the whole world, be given to a person that neither showed any interest in them, nor seemed to be spiritually qualified? Rebekah had most likely also told Jacob which of the two God had chosen. The pot of stew was Jacob’s test to find out how much the calling meant to Esau. Esau considered the satisfaction of his hunger to be of greater importance than God’s eternal calling.

From this story, the Book of Hebrews warns us—not about what Jacob did, but about what Esau did. It does not say, “See to it that you do not act like Jacob.” It says rather, “See to it …that no one is sexually immoral or unholy like Esau, who sold his birthright for a single meal.” (Heb 12:15-16) Jacob fought his whole life for the birthright. Esau despised it. The Torah says of Esau, “he ate and drank and rose and went his way. Thus Esau despised his birthright.” (v. 34) Esau’s example is a warning against being someone who primarily lives for selfish pleasures and carnal desires.

In the next chapter of the Torah, it says that Esau chose to marry two Canaanite women. “When Esau was forty years old, he took Judith the daughter of Beeri the Hittite to be his wife, and Basemath the daughter of Elon the Hittite, and they made life bitter for Isaac and Rebekah.” (Gen 26:34-35) This demonstrates how ignorant Esau was about spiritual matters, and how little he valued them. He was also very selfish and insensitive, since he did not realize how grievous his behavior was to Isaac and Rebekah until many years later, when Isaac blessed Jacob and sent him away to get a bride from Abraham’s relatives.

“Now Esau saw that Isaac had blessed Jacob and sent him away to Paddan-aram to take a wife from there, and that as he blessed him he directed him, ‘You must not take a wife from the Canaanite women,’ and that Jacob had obeyed his father and his mother and gone to Paddan-aram. So when Esau saw that the Canaanite women did not please Isaac his father, Esau went to Ishmael and took as his wife, besides the wives he had, Mahalath the daughter of Ishmael, Abraham’s son, the sister of Nebaioth.” (Gen 28:6-9)

Esau, however, never repented. He simply added one more wife to his harem. The unholy and sexually immoral son of Isaac married the daughter of the unholy and sexually immoral son of Abraham. This marriage only made the situation worse, but Esau did not understand this. He was completely ignorant of spiritual things.
